These exercises practise the ideas from Chapter 5: centre, spread, shape, unusual values, missing data, and correlation. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
library(dplyr)
students  <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
questionnaire <- read.csv("questionnaire.csv")
first_sem <- semesters |>
  filter(semester == 1) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id))
```

## Centre, spread, and shape

### Exercise 1: Four summaries

Calculate the mean, median, SD, and IQR of first-semester `study_hours`. Are the mean and median close? Which pair of summaries would you report?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
first_sem |>
  summarise(
    mean   = mean(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = ______(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd     = ______(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr    = ______(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
first_sem |>
  summarise(
    mean   = mean(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd     = sd(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr    = IQR(study_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

The mean (about 28 hours) is a little above the median (26 hours): study hours are only mildly skewed. The mean and SD are acceptable here; the median and IQR would also be fine.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: Is wellbeing normal?

Draw a Q-Q plot of first-semester `wellbeing` with base R's `qqnorm()`, and add the reference line with `qqline()`. Do the points follow the line?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
qqnorm(first_sem$______)
qqline(first_sem$______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
qqnorm(first_sem$wellbeing)
qqline(first_sem$wellbeing)
```

The points follow the line closely: wellbeing is approximately normal.
:::
:::

## Unusual values and missing data

### Exercise 3: The box plot rule

How many students have unusually high first-semester `study_hours` by the box plot rule (above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR$)?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
x  <- first_sem$study_hours
q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
fence <- q3 + 1.5 * ______(x, na.rm = TRUE)
fence
sum(x > ______, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
x  <- first_sem$study_hours
q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
fence <- q3 + 1.5 * IQR(x, na.rm = TRUE)
fence
sum(x > fence, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Just one: the upper fence is 65.5 hours, and one student studies 67 hours a week. Study hours have almost no outliers, unlike caffeine.
:::
:::

### Exercise 4: Who left the study?

Compare the first-semester sleep of students who later left the study with those who stayed. Is there a difference?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
left_ids <- setdiff(students$student_id,
                    semesters$student_id[semesters$semester == 3])
first_sem |>
  mutate(left_study = student_id %in% ______) |>
  summarise(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE), students = n(),
            .by = ______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
left_ids <- setdiff(students$student_id,
                    semesters$student_id[semesters$semester == 3])
first_sem |>
  mutate(left_study = student_id %in% left_ids) |>
  summarise(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE), students = n(),
            .by = left_study)
```

Almost no difference: about 6.4 hours for those who left and 6.5 for those who stayed. The students who left differed in wellbeing and in thoughts of dropping out (as the chapter showed), but not in sleep. Missing data can be related to some variables and not others, so check each one you use.
:::
:::

## Relationships

### Exercise 5: Support and satisfaction

Calculate each student's support and satisfaction scores, then the correlation between them. Using Cohen's guidelines (0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large), how strong is it?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
scores <- questionnaire |>
  mutate(
    support      = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    satisfaction = rowMeans(pick(______), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
cor(scores$support, scores$______, use = "complete.obs")
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The satisfaction items are `satisfaction_1` to `satisfaction_4`: `pick(satisfaction_1:satisfaction_4)`.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
scores <- questionnaire |>
  mutate(
    support      = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    satisfaction = rowMeans(pick(satisfaction_1:satisfaction_4), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
cor(scores$support, scores$satisfaction, use = "complete.obs")
```

About 0.4: a medium-to-large correlation. Students who feel supported by their supervisor are more satisfied with their programme. But this does not show that support *causes* satisfaction: satisfied students might also see their supervisors more positively, or something else might affect both.
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: Describe the sample

Complete the summary of Elaf's sample: the number of students, the percentage who study part-time, and the mean and SD of age.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
first_sem |>
  summarise(
    students      = n(),
    part_time_pct = 100 * mean(study_mode == ______),
    age_mean      = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    age_sd        = ______
  )
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
first_sem |>
  summarise(
    students      = n(),
    part_time_pct = 100 * mean(study_mode == "Part-time"),
    age_mean      = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    age_sd        = sd(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
:::
:::
